Gaming_Tech.title: Value of Google parent Alphabet plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
Gaming_Tech.text:
Google parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations.

Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue.

Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race.

But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.

At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.

Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.

However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.

Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.

By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.

Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter.

The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.

Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."

Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.

Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.

Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.

That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.

Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.

Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.

"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."

As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.

"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."

Gaming_Tech.title: The Traitors: Bombshell confession as faithfuls finally turn the screw
Gaming_Tech.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

With the traitors still riding high following last Friday's episode, could they really just walk it to the final? It was time to find out.

Having been bestowed with the almighty power of the double dagger - well, metaphorically speaking, at least - King Kenny held all the cards, choosing to use his special power of a double vote to send another faithful packing.

As cliffhangers go, it wasn't hugely thrilling for viewers at home, given that the pair up for banishment - Sharon Rooney and Joanne McNally - were both faithfuls.

Nevertheless, it left a big impact on the faithful crew as they realised they had let the traitors land yet another blow ahead of Friday's final.

"We've got to pull something out of the bag," said frustrated faithful Michael Sheen later. He wasn't wrong.

Joanne got teary as she departed and joked "she was premenstrual," before revealing she was "a hardcore faithful".

Maya described her as a "ball of fun", while Kenny put on his best acting skills in the aftermath by pretending to be struggling with having the deciding vote, even comforting poor Sharon. Give that man an Oscar.

Meanwhile, James Blunt was on the hunt for whiskey like a teenager at the end of a house party: "Where do they keep the stiff stuff?" he asked himself, finding only a tray of empty glasses.

Murder was soon on the minds of the traitors again as the dastardly trio of Kenny, Maya and James A trudged up to the turret.

"The life of a traitor... it's not for everyone," said Maya. And that probably includes James A, although to be fair, he has shown a bit more enthusiasm for some pantomime villainy in the last couple of episodes. More on him later.

"Let's have faith," said King Kenny without a hint of irony.

As ever, James B was as far off the pace as me in the year 11 cross-country race.

When Leigh-Anne Pinnock, probably the most astute faithful of the series, brought up James A being a potential traitor over breakfast, James B sarcastically replied: "I think that's a good theory to start banishing the most innocent."

Sharon - aka Poundland Poirot - failed to appear in the dining room, having been chosen for the chopping block so soon after escaping banishment, throwing all the faithfuls into more confusion. She was getting a bit stressed, so it was probably for the best.

Michael had a warning for the traitors though, giving his most rousing oratory since his motivational speech for the Welsh football team ahead of the 2022 World Cup.

"Traitors... today is going to be a living hell for you, I am going to push and push and push and you are going to suffer today. This is the apocalypse.

"Vengeful daddy is in the house today."

Theories were soon flying left right and centre, with Bash throwing the spotlight on "the head of the round table" Michael, Kenny putting suspicion on James B, while Romesh pointed the finger at actual traitor Maya, shock, horror.

And the obsession with the peacock perfume wasn't going anywhere.

Finally Michael 'Vengeful Daddy' Sheen seemed to be on to something, telling a shell-shocked Maya in the kitchen: "I think you could be a brilliant traitor, and if you and Kenny paired up, amazing."

She was probably relieved when the jeeps turned up for another day trip, and Romesh was all of us with his hilarious reaction to news of yet another insane mission.

On being told by host Claudia Winkleman that they had to find the severed heads of some of the murdered celebrities and reunite them with the head of the buried body, he got the giggles: "It's just so ridiculous. I love it though!"

James B tried to get one group in the Frankenstein-style lab to sing his hit Beautiful - which had Leigh-Ann and Michael bopping along but by the puzzled look on Kenny's face, he had clearly never heard it. Awks.

This mission was a bit of a rehash of the wailing in the well challenge from the first Celebrity Traitors series, with Claudia going full headteacher and cheering - or should we say, shouting - the teams on.

Digital versions of the dead celebs in bell jars had to be matched to the correct gravestone in the castle gardens.

"Seeing Ross's face when he was alive was enough to give a man pause, let alone when his dismembered head is looking out at you from a pickle jar," quipped Michael.

Back at the castle, it seemed that Michael wasn't the only one starting to turn up the heat on Maya.

Romesh and Bash decided she had gone under the radar long enough: "One of the greatest gliders in the game. Maybe Olympic level gliding," mused Bash. And King Kenny was also in their sights.

And so to the penultimate round table. (A shout out to Claudia's sequin-tastic midnight blue trouser suit).

Michael was under the spotlight first due to his presence, intelligence and status as "the father of the table."

In turn, he first went back to his previous suspicion of Leigh-Anne on the night of the murder in plain sight, accusing her again of using her Big Mix dance with Miranda as a distraction.

Romesh put heat on James B due to his vocal accusations, which were often wrong.

The quiet ones - traitors James A and Maya - were then questioned by Michael and James B, who soon honed in on the murder in plain sight, working out that Maya, Kenny and James A were in the library at the end of the night when Ross was killed.

Vengeful Daddy was indeed in the house, and James B was on the money for once. Credit where it's due.

Then the bombshell of the series - something that has never happened before in the history of the show.

James A, who failed dismally to defend himself against Michael's accusations, clearly couldn't take any more and confessed he was a traitor at the table.

"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.

"I've had a unique experience on this that no-one has had before, I wanted to be a faithful and that's all I wanted to be. But I couldn't just say 'guys, vote for me.'"

At least no-one had to explain their decision when they all wrote his name down on the boards.

And as Michael and Maya stood round the firepit before heading to bed - or the turret in Maya's case - she looked like a dead woman walking. And DSI Sheen is on her case.

Gaming_Tech.title: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.

Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.

Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.

The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise, external from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.

The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.

However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.

Total welfare spending would also remain below the peak of around 12% of GDP in 2013 following the global financial crisis, leading some economists and researchers to question the idea that welfare spending is out of control., external

But there are some welfare costs that are rising rapidly.

Spending on health and disability related benefits, in particular Personal Independence Payments (PIP), is up sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Accounting for inflation, spending on working-age disability benefits increased from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026, external.

Inflation-adjusted welfare spending remains lower than 2013 because several other working-age benefits, such as Universal Credit and housing benefit, were cut by Conservative-led governments as part of their austerity programme from 2010 onwards, external.

So spending in some parts of the system has come down while it has risen in others - and there could be a connection.

Some researchers think the post-2010 welfare cuts to benefits might have created an incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead to protect their living standards, external, therefore shifting costs around the system rather than generating lasting savings.

Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many off benefits and into work.

His interim report in May estimated that annual PIP expenditure on 16 to 24-year-olds rose from £1.3bn in 2020 to around £3.2bn in 2025, external. It also projected this cost would reach £6.5bn and cover 700,000 young people in five years' time.

PIP claimants can be in work, but official statistics show that only around one in five are, external.

Politicians are often unclear about what they mean by reducing spending on welfare.

In March 2025, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government presented a plan which it said would save £5bn a year from health-related welfare spending by 2030 by tightening PIP access and reducing the value of health-related Universal Credit payments.

But official forecasts made it clear that annual spending on health-related welfare in cash terms was still set to rise after the reform, external, just not as rapidly as the path it had previously been on.

However, at the time the OBR did forecast the plans would help put overall UK welfare spending on a "slightly downward trajectory" as a share of the economy, external over the medium term, rather than remaining flat as had been previously projected.

So this type of relative reduction in anticipated welfare spending, rather than a cut in absolute cash terms, could be what the government seeks to deliver.

The final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.

There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25, external, so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.

There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access, external, although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.

Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.

But some analysts argue that to be effective in delivering sustainable savings, such reforms are likely also to require the government to spend a lot more, external to enable young people in particular to get into and remain in work.

This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits, suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.

This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.

However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.

Gaming_Tech.title: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
Gaming_Tech.text:
Eating fruit and vegetable scraps such as peels and stalks could provide a health boost that most of us are missing, say UK researchers, external.

They say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre and are encouraging people to try "root-to-tip" eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds.

Most adults do not get enough fibre. Official figures, external show only 4% meet the recommended 30g a day, despite its well-known benefits for gut health.

Fibre aids digestion, helps you feel fuller for longer and is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer., external

As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides.

Eating a kiwi with the skin on, external provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example.

For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon.

They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.

watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal bread

butternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakes

pineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the flesh

broccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the florets

Fibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.

Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre.

"This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one; you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."

The college has been experimenting in its canteen, external, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.

At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries, or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.

While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.

Steaming, microwaving, or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best.

Dr Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."

She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try.

Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.

Over the nine-week period, 'root-to-tip' dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.

Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.

Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.

She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.

Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.

"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.

She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people with IBS may find it harder to tolerate.

And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.

Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

Gaming_Tech.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand options for customers
Gaming_Tech.text:
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.

DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.

Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.

"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.

"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.

For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.

He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".

The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.

Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.

"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.

In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.

DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.

The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.

New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."

"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

Gaming_Tech.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.

Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."

"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.

"We will update the public when more information is available."

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.

The information was put in a database named Icepick.

Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.

Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.

BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.

A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.

Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.

The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.

Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.

A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."

Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.

In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.

Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.

Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.

Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement.

Gaming_Tech.title: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
Gaming_Tech.text:
Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.

On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).

Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.

Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.

The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.

Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres.

Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.

Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.

The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.

The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."

Gaming_Tech.title: Elon Musk a 'real genius', Putin says after talks with SpaceX boss
Gaming_Tech.text:
Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.

The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.

"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."

Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.

Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".

"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.

Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.

The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".

"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.

Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.

US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.

Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.

Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".

Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.

Gaming_Tech.title: Drone technology: Start-ups look for ways to make quieter drones
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nature lover Ashley Schmidt no longer spends much time in her garden, in the Dallas suburb of North Garland.

She's also given up on cycling to the local parks where she previously enjoyed taking close-up photos of the bugs, lizards and toads.

It's all because she can't stand the sound of the delivery drones that fly overhead, depositing her neighbours' online orders.

"They emit this very annoying buzz. It triggers my fight or flight response," says the 44-year-old administrative assistant.

"You can hear the drones on approach and you can hear them inside your home when they pass directly overhead and then you hear them as they leave," she says.

Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.

Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.

Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.

Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.

While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.

Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.

"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.

Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?

One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.

The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.

Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.

Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.

Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.

For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.

He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – except that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.

"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"

The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.

"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

Gaming_Tech.title: iPhone Duo: Apple to replace handsets affected by screen issues
Gaming_Tech.text:
Apple has acknowledged some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.

Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device, which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.

Apple said it was aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.

The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, is an attempt to reinvigorate the brand's device range and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.

Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.

The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using AI.

Francisco Jeronimo, technology analyst at market research firm IDC, said that meant some caution was needed before drawing conclusions about the whole production run.

But he added the early reports of issues also showed "that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables".

Gaming_Tech.title: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO
Gaming_Tech.text:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.

Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.

"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.

Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.

The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

Gaming_Tech.title: Data centre backlash grows ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know
Gaming_Tech.text:
Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.

As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.

Entertainment.title: Sir Patrick Stewart: Actor who moved effortlessly between Star Trek and Shakespeare
Entertainment.text:
Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, was a stage and screen great who balanced Hollywood stardom with an equally stellar career in classical theatre.

While many actors are typecast, he moved effortlessly from Shakespeare and Dickens to the command of the USS Enterprise and his famous wheelchair in X-Men.

In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.

One of the world's most versatile actors, he mastered both comedy and tragedy, science-fiction and historical drama - despite the entertainment industry's traditional dislike of bald heads.

Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire on 13 July 1940.

His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.

His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had shredded his mental health.

"My father was a very potent individual," Stewart later recalled. "It was said that when he strode on to the parade ground, birds stopped singing."

But Alfred Stewart had become a quick-tempered man, suffering from what would now be called post traumatic stress.

He was prone to drink and often took out his frustrations on his family - although Patrick himself was never the target of his fists.

Young Patrick's love of drama developed at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.

His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.

He found the predictability of dramatic performances a welcome change from the turmoil of his home life.

He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a journalist and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.

He also threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."

But he found it impossible to concentrate on both his job and his acting. Eventually his editor told him to choose between journalism and the "foolhardy" acting.

Stewart picked up his typewriter and walked out.

At the age of 18, he had the traumatic experience of losing all his hair, a huge blow to an aspiring actor and self-conscious teenager - who worried that girls would no longer find him attractive.

He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company - playing a variety of roles across the company's repertoire.

And when not appearing as Oberon or Enobarbus, he made his TV debut as a fireman in a 1967 episode of soap opera Coronation Street.

In 1984, Stewart left the RSC and moved to the National Theatre. By then in his mid-40s, he had only ever been unemployed for three weeks, but was rarely cast as a main character.

He had landed a number of supporting film roles: including playing Guinevere's father in Excalibur, a minstrel in Dune, and a riding instructor in Little Lord Fauntleroy.

And he was the voice of a small character in the animated film of Richard Adams' novel The Plague Dogs.

But even he described the first half of his career as "sound but never spectacular".

Then came the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

A producer named Robert L Justman was intent on reviving the Star Trek franchise, and was looking for a successor to William Shatner's legendary James T Kirk.

He had hoped to find a sexy, hirsute Frenchman to play the role - but chanced upon Stewart giving a lecture to his wife's Shakespeare class in Los Angeles.

Justman turned to his wife. "I said I think I've found our new captain," he said.

Stewart was intrigued but sceptical.

He knew nothing about the original Star Trek and his great friend, Sir Ian McKellen, told him not to throw his stage career away on a wild goose chase into space.

But in need of a boost to his finances, Stewart signed a six-year contract, firmly believing the show wouldn't last and he'd be back on the boards before long.

"Everybody told me it would be a flop," he recalled. "A friend of mine said, 'Get a suntan, make some money, go home.'"

He was, however, pleased that the producers didn't mind his baldness.

He'd tried wearing a wig in early screen tests, but it looked ratty and - in the end - Star Trek's founder Gene Roddenberry told him to ditch it.

"In the 24th Century, they wouldn't care if Picard was bald," he said.

Stewart, who was billed by the New York Times as "an unknown British Shakespearean actor", found it hard adapting to his new job.

After his stage experiences, he found the 20 hours a day on set tiring, and he also struggled to work with a fairly laid-back and fun-loving US cast.

His decision to call his fellow actors together and give them a lecture about behaving more seriously failed to gain him popularity.

"It was really awful, being dressed down by the captain," said Brent Spiner, who played Data, the android. "We really thought, 'Well, please, get over it'."

Eventually Stewart softened, insisting that every member of the cast told at least one joke a day.

Despite his initial reservations, Star Trek: The Next Generation both survived and prospered - making its star a very wealthy man.

Captain Picard was supposed to be French, but displayed a surprisingly English regard for both Shakespeare and Earl Grey tea.

And, after playing all those Shakespearean princes and dukes on the London stage, Stewart became fiercely proud of him, and of the show's ability to connect with younger audiences.

In addition to the television series, Stewart played Picard in four Star Trek films. But while commanding the Enterprise, he managed to not neglect the theatre.

With his new-found celebrity, the parts he was offered improved greatly.

For years, he performed a one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol on Broadway - playing all 40 characters.

In 1995, he appeared as Prospero in a memorable performance of The Tempest and, two years later, he starred as Othello - who he presented as a white mercenary in a black African nation.

But his Star Trek success limited the roles that Hollywood was prepared to offer him.

"No director wanted to cast this grand, deep-voiced, bald English guy," he told the Times. "Because everybody knew he was Picard and couldn't possibly be anybody else."

In 2009, he again teamed up with Sir Ian in Waiting For Godot.

It was a moment of personal fulfilment for Sir Patrick who, as an awed teenager, remembered watching Peter O'Toole in the play at the Bristol Old Vic.

His deep and authoritative voice made him much in demand for voice-over roles - including a reprise of his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek video games.

One female interviewer once gushed that "just hearing him order breakfast is rather thrilling".

He also voiced a host of TV commercials both in Britain and the US.

Away from acting, he was a passionate political activist and a long-time supporter of the Labour Party, as well as a campaigner for victims of domestic abuse.

In 2013, he married his third wife - singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell - in Nevada.

Sir Ian McKellen officiated at the ceremony, which had to be restaged at a Los Angeles restaurant when someone discovered that his legal power to do so did not extend to the Silver State.

A year later, the two knights took their talents to Broadway, alternating performances of Waiting for Godot with Harold Pinter's No Man's Land.

Sir Patrick made a video for Amnesty International on the subject of domestic violence, referencing his father's brutality towards his mother.

Once named the third greatest Yorkshireman after Michael Palin and Sean Bean, he never lost touch with his roots - keeping a house in God's Own Country, and remaining a lifelong supporter of Huddersfield Town football club.

Forthcoming projects had included a final performance as Professor Charles Xavier in Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday, which will be released this Christmas.

And, if millions remember him only as the somewhat taciturn commander of the USS Enterprise, that prospect was not something that worried him.

"For huge numbers of people I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that's fine," he said. "I really believe we created an admirable individual."

While many actors are typecast, he moved effortlessly from Shakespeare and Dickens to the command of the USS Enterprise and his famous wheelchair in...

Entertainment.title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
Entertainment.text:
Warning: This story contains graphic content.

Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

The 39-year-old told the jury at his rape and sexual assault trial that "the way he treats me is to know me", adding: "I feel very seen by him... I love him very much."

The media personality faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday, Laura Brand was asked by the defence barrister if her husband respected her when she didn't want to be sexual with him, and she replied: "Yes absolutely."

Laura Brand is the daughter of former golfer Bernard Gallacher and sister of TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher. She married Brand in 2017 and they have three children.

She told the court she first met him at the Edinburgh festival in 2006, explaining that he took her number and they started a relationship soon afterwards.

She said that after his performance: "I went over and said, 'I'm Laura, Kirsty's sister. That was a great show'."

He contacted her the next day, she said. When they met, she said they had oral sex, adding: "He might have wanted to have sex but I didn't want to."

Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others.

"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.

"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."

She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.

Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."

Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.

"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."

The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.

He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."

Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.

He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".

He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".

On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends

Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".

She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".

"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.

Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.

Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.

"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.

She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.

The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

Entertainment.title: George Michael's Faith guitar sells for £180k after auction row
Entertainment.text:
The guitar George Michael performed with in his 1987 Faith music video has sold for £180,000 at auction, after a row over the sale of memorabilia related to the singer.

The guitar was one of more than 30 items auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant. The sale fetched a total of £238,000 excluding buyers' premium.

Bailey died in 2014 and the items were sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.

Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Belcher declined to comment.

Sworders chairman Guy Schooling said Belcher had been "nothing but delightful" during their interactions over the past two-and-a-half years.

"There are two ways of looking at this - it can be cashing in, or it can be a bit of a memorial and a tribute to Siobhan, and that's the way we've looked at it," he told BBC News.

The auction house billed the 32 lots, including signed photographs, invitations to events and presentation CDs and discs, as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".

Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.

Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.

There is no suggestion that Belcher did not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.

Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.

In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considered the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name was "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".

He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" was "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".

Bailey asked that the auction should not go ahead, or be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.

Siobhan Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.

She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.

"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.

"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."

The guitar was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.

The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".

£180,000 - The Rockabilly Rebel guitar from the Faith video, with original hardshell case and leather guitar strap

£7,000 - A Queen Five Live EP sleeve signed by Brian May, John Deacon, Roger Taylor, George Michael and Lisa Stansfield

£5,000 - A Faith Tour ringbound itinerary from George Michael's 1988 world tour

£4,800 - A presentation CD of George Michael's Older

£4,500 - A gold disc of Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go

£4,200 - A gold disc of George Michael's I Want Your Sex

Other items on sale included a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Andrew Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.

"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.

Speaking before Thursday's auction, he said "she would never have consented" to it, adding that the sale "breaks my heart".

"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax [tour itinerary] and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.

Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".

He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".

Bailey acknowledged that Belcher had a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

George Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.

Entertainment.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
Entertainment.text:
The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.

The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.

Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.

The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.

"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.

Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

Entertainment.title: Ex-Top Gear host Richard Hammond's new Abergavenny life wild swimming and food festivals
Entertainment.text:
Former Top Gear star Richard Hammond says he has swapped vintage cars for food festivals and running as he settles into life in a Welsh market town.

The 56-year-old bought a £2m Georgian mansion in Llanwenarth, near Abergavenny in Monmouthshire, in November 2025 following his divorce from wife Mindy after 23 years.

The presenter previously told BBC Wales he had "never been happier" since moving into the 19th Century home, and each week he has discovered a new reason to be "delighted that I live there".

With Bannau Brycheiniog - Brecon Beacons - in his back garden, Hammond told the High Performance Podcast he had taken up open water swimming as he becomes "braver" than he has ever been.

Hammond said it only took him a couple of visits to the property for him to realise that he "loved it".

"The Brecon Beacons National Park is the other side of my right-hand fence," he told the Telegraph.

"I can walk up the Sugar Loaf Mountain in an hour and 20 minutes or I could be getting measured for a new suit or buying a coffee in 20 minutes."

His home is currently being renovated to include car garages, a padel court and guest accommodation.

He recently made headlines for saying he would "find a way" to share his space with rare bats that have paused his renovation plans.

He said: "I just have to work with the bats. I like bats. You don't move to where I've moved and try to stamp all the nature out."

At the beginning of 2025, Hammond announced that he and his wife Mindy, who share two children, were separating, just three months after his father died of cancer.

It also came around the time of the final Grand Tour episode which brought his 22-year broadcasting career with Jeremy Clarkson and James May to an end.

Since then, he has been rebuilding his life in Wales, and said his energy levels had "been replenished".

"I'm now far braver and do things I would never have done," he said.

He has even joined an Abergavenny running club, bringing his 5k time down to under 25 minutes, and taken up open water swimming in the Lake District as he keeps pace with new girlfriend Keira "Kiki" Glen.

"Basically, she did a triathlon and I went to support her," he told the Telegraph.

"They were all having such a great time and buzzing afterwards, so I signed up for next year and got swept along."

While you would expect that classic cars and motor racing still feature heavily in his life, Hammond is aware that his priorities have shifted.

Rather than attending the Goodwood Revival festival this year, he was sampling cheeses and whiskies at the Abergavenny Food Festival.

Hammond's daughter Izzy has inherited her father's love of cars and the pair now co-present on the social media channel DriveTribe.

Hammond said he was "sure" she would be interested in a role on Top Gear some day.

"It'd be good to see some females on those shows," he said.

"Half the drivers are. TV has a role to play in representation. It's important, nobody's going to step into an arena unless they see somebody that represents them."

Entertainment.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
Entertainment.text:
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.

The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.

Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".

"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.

"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."

China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.

Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.

Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.

Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.

State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".

Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."

When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".

Entertainment.title: Northants actor Robert Rhodes targets 'scarred villain'stereotype
Entertainment.text:
An actor is backing a charity's call for more positive roles for performers with scars and visible differences.

Northamptonshire-based Robert Rhodes, who has appeared in Silent Witness and House of the Dragon, said: "The media industry needs to start reflecting the true experience of people with visible difference."

The charity Changing Faces wants the film and TV industry to stop using scars, burns and other visible differences as marks of villainy and has started a petition calling for more positive representation.

One casting agency said visible differences were often used as a shorthand for villainy, but that these casting briefs could be successfully challenged.

New research by the Centre for Appearance Research (CAR) at the University of the West of England showed that people who are exposed to visible difference via villainous characters go on to have a more negative perception of people with visible difference in the real world, the charity said.

Rhodes, who was recently in the BBC One show, The Rapture, was born with a large facial birthmark as a result of congenital melanocytic nevus and was left with scarring following multiple surgeries to remove it as a child.

He said: "We can't wait for action any longer.

"Yes, there is often trauma associated with a scar, but we experience joy, love and success just like everyone else.

"More neutral and aspirational characters on screen will improve real perceptions of the whole visible difference community."

Fellow actor Beau Bradfield said: "As an actor with facial scarring, I know how important it is to see people with visible differences represented on screen as real, complex people.

"I want children growing up with visible differences to see characters who look like them being heroes, friends, parents and love interests – not just villains."

About 4.9 million people in the UK have a visible difference, the charity said.

As part of its work to monitor visible difference representation, it has worked with the Creative Diversity Network to include visible difference as a category in its diversity data monitoring and reporting.

Louise Wright, chief executive of Changing Faces, said: "For years we've asked the industry to think about the stories it tells about visible difference.

"Now, for the first time, we have proof that those stories don't stay on screen – they shape how people with visible difference are treated in real life.

"Halloween is the moment this is impossible to ignore, which is why we're asking industry, and the public, to help us change it."

Bailey Frances, from Cambridge-based Shakyra Dowling Casting, a member of the Casting Directors' Association, said: "Getting it right matters.

"Villains are often written with visible differences (eg facial scars) as shorthand, but asking whether a character could be interpreted differently, or whether that difference is essential to the story, leads to better, more truthful storytelling," she said.

"We regularly present actors who don't match the description on the page but fit the character perfectly, and they're often the ones who get the job.

"Casting directors are in a unique position to widen the search and open up the conversation with writers and directors, challenging the initial casting briefs where needed."

Entertainment.title: Sam Fender's Newcastle pre-sale moved after 'bot attack'
Entertainment.text:
Sam Fender has rescheduled the pre-sale for his tour's homecoming show after a "sophisticated bot attack" reportedly affected a ticketing website.

In a post on Instagram, the 32-year-old said he had been told the site Gigantic had been hit for his shows at St James' Park in Newcastle in summer 2027, prompting him to move the sale back 24 hours to 09:30 GMT on Thursday.

It came days after he removed a ticket category from sale due to his unhappiness with the costs for fans, which he said were out of his control.

Gigantic said its system had detected an "unusually high volume of suspicious activity" resulting in error messages on its site and it had halted the pre-sale to protect fans.

Fender announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour last week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester.

The musician from North Shields did not give details for any other venues being affected by the "bot attack", but a source told the BBC they did not have any issues buying tickets for the London show.

Fender wrote: "Being told that there's been a sophisticated bot attack to the Gigantic ticket site which is impacting the St James' Park pre-sale.

"We're going to have to move the Newcastle pre-sale to 09:30 tomorrow to ensure real fans get the tickets."

Gigantic said in a statement: "We know how frustrating this morning was for many of you, and we're sorry.

"Fans should be able to buy tickets fairly, and that is what we're working to make sure happens."

Entertainment.title: Budget 2026: Liverpool Littlewoods film studios to get £20m boost
Entertainment.text:
The government has pledged £20m towards plans to transform Liverpool's derelict Littlewoods building into a film and television production campus.

The funding, announced in the Budget earlier, will come from the government's Growth Mission Fund but is subject to final business case approval.

The long-delayed project would see the former Littlewoods Pools headquarters on Edge Lane turned into a 260,000 sq ft (six-acre, 2.4-hectare) creative campus for film, television, gaming and other digital screen industries.

It is unclear whether the money will be enough to meet the project's funding needs - Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram previously sought £50m in government support.

Plans to turn the landmark Art Deco building into a film and television complex have been discussed since 2017 but have faced repeated delays.

In February, Rotheram said he was "desperate" to get the project "off the ground", but acknowledged a funding gap.

At the time, the Liverpool City Region Combined Authority had committed up to £17m towards the scheme.

Developer Capital & Centric had previously warned that the cost of delivering the project "in the current climate exceeds the value of the completed development".

Liverpool City Council said the new investment would support the wider redevelopment of the site, known as the Liverpool Creative Campus.
